## Sensitivity and identifiability — Day 2, Session 3

Worksheet: `worksheets/chapters/14-sensitivity-and-identifiability.qmd`. The
chapter is [Sensitivity and
identifiability](../chapters/14-sensitivity-and-identifiability.qmd).

Parameters travel as the plain vector `p0 = [β, c, γ]` here rather than as a
named tuple, because sensitivity analysis differentiates with respect to the
parameter *vector*: column 1 means $\beta$ because $\beta$ is first.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-setup
using CairoMakie
using GlobalSensitivity
using Logging
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using SciMLSensitivity
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

# The Sobol sampler prints a design-matrix warning on every call.
Logging.disable_logging(Logging.Warn)

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

N = 1000.0
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p0 = [0.05, 10.0, 0.25]          # β, c, γ
tgrid = collect(0.0:0.25:40.0)

function sir_kernel!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ = p
    S, I, R = u
    incidence = β * c * S * I / N
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    return nothing
end

println("R₀ = ", p0[1] * p0[2] / p0[3])
```

### Part B — reading a sensitivity matrix

Scaling each derivative by its own parameter answers a question you can ask of
all three at once: if this parameter were raised by 1% of its own value, how many
people would $I$ move by? The finite difference then checks the derivative by
moving $\gamma$ and looking.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-b1
sensitivity_problem = ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), p0)
sensitivity_solution = solve(sensitivity_problem, Tsit5();
                             saveat = tgrid, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9)
states, jacobians = extract_local_sensitivities(sensitivity_solution, true)
final_jacobian = jacobians[end]

scaled = [final_jacobian[2, j] * p0[j] for j in 1:3]

check("β and c have the same scaled sensitivity",
      abs(scaled[1] - scaled[2]) < 1e-8)

(; unscaled = round.(final_jacobian[2, :]; digits = 3),
   scaled = round.(scaled; digits = 3))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-b2
ε = 1e-5
perturbed = copy(p0)
perturbed[3] += ε

perturbed_solution = solve(ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), perturbed),
                           Tsit5(); saveat = tgrid, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9)

finite_difference = (Array(perturbed_solution)[2, end] - states[2, end]) / ε
jacobian_entry = final_jacobian[2, 3]

check("the finite difference agrees with the Jacobian",
      abs(finite_difference - jacobian_entry) / (1 + abs(jacobian_entry)) < 1e-3)

(; finite_difference, jacobian_entry)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch14-local
#| fig-cap: "Local derivatives of the infectious state with respect to each parameter, scaled by the parameter value so the three are comparable."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "∂I/∂θ × θ")
for (j, (name, colour)) in enumerate(zip(["β", "c", "γ"],
                                         [:steelblue, :darkorange, :seagreen]))
    lines!(ax, tgrid, [jac[2, j] * p0[j] for jac in jacobians];
           label = name, linewidth = j == 2 ? 4 : 2,
           linestyle = j == 2 ? :dash : :solid, color = colour)
end
axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
fig
```

#### B1. Interpret

- In `sir_kernel!` the two parameters appear only as the product `β * c`, never
  apart, so $I(t)$ is a function of $\beta c$. The chain rule gives $\partial
  I/\partial\beta = c\,\partial I/\partial(\beta c)$ and $\partial I/\partial c =
  \beta\,\partial I/\partial(\beta c)$, and multiplying each by its own parameter
  turns both into $\beta c\,\partial I/\partial(\beta c)$ — which is why the
  scaled values agree to about $10^{-14}$ at every saved time, not just the end.
- The model cannot distinguish a contact rate of 10 with transmission probability
  0.05 from a contact rate of 20 with probability 0.025. Part D proves this is a
  property of the model and the observation, not of this parameter vector.
- The sign change is about what a derivative measures: the effect on the *level
  of $I$ at that time*, not on the epidemic as a whole. Raising transmission makes
  the epidemic grow faster, so through the growth phase $I$ is higher; by day 40
  the faster epidemic has already burned through the susceptibles and has fewer
  infectious people left, so the derivative is negative.
- A single number like $\partial I(40)/\partial\beta$ is meaningless without
  saying which time it refers to.

### Part C — global sensitivity and the output you choose

Timing needs a decision that peak size does not: peak of *what*, measured *when*?
`peak_of` locates the model's own peak with a `ContinuousCallback` watching
$\beta cS/N - \gamma$, while `scheduled_prevalence_peak` reports what a survey on
a fixed schedule would say.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-c1
function peak_of(p)
    β, c, γ = Float64.(p)
    # I is already falling at t = 0, so its maximum is there.
    β * c * u0[1] / N <= γ && return (time = 0.0, size = u0[2])
    peak = Ref((time = 0.0, size = u0[2]))
    growth_rate(u, t, integrator) = β * c * u[1] / N - γ
    record_peak!(integrator) =
        (peak[] = (time = integrator.t, size = integrator.u[2]))
    solve(ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 80.0), [β, c, γ]), Tsit5();
          callback = ContinuousCallback(growth_rate, record_peak!),
          save_everystep = false, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
    return peak[]
end

peak_time(p) = peak_of(p).time
peak_size(p) = peak_of(p).size

function scheduled_prevalence_peak(p; measurement_interval = 0.25)
    times = 0.0:measurement_interval:80.0
    solution = solve(ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 80.0), Float64.(p)),
                     Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
    prevalence = Array(solution)[2, :]
    return times[argmax(prevalence)]
end

parameter_bounds = [[0.02, 0.08],   # β
                    [5.0, 15.0],    # c
                    [0.15, 0.40]]   # γ

println("model peak time : ", round(peak_time(p0); digits = 2))
for interval in (0.25, 1.0, 7.0)
    println("measured every ", lpad(interval, 4), " days: ",
            scheduled_prevalence_peak(p0; measurement_interval = interval))
end
```

Growth on day zero needs $\mathcal{R}_0 S(0)/N > 1$ rather than
$\mathcal{R}_0 > 1$, so the no-epidemic corner of the box is
$\mathcal{R}_0 \le N/S(0) \approx 1.0101$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-c2
rng = StableRNG(7)
draws = 20_000
no_growth = N / u0[1]
sampled_R₀ = [(0.02 + 0.06 * rand(rng)) * (5.0 + 10.0 * rand(rng)) /
              (0.15 + 0.25 * rand(rng)) for _ in 1:draws]
println("share of the box that never grows: ",
        round(100 * mean(sampled_R₀ .<= no_growth); digits = 1), "%")
println("peak time there: ", peak_time([0.02, 5.0, 0.40]))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-c3
size_indices = gsa(peak_size, Sobol(), parameter_bounds; samples = 200)
println("peak size  | S1 = ", round.(size_indices.S1; digits = 3),
        " | ST = ", round.(size_indices.ST; digits = 3))

time_indices = Dict{Int, Any}()
for n in (32, 200, 1000)
    time_indices[n] = gsa(peak_time, Sobol(), parameter_bounds; samples = n)
    println("peak time, ", lpad(n, 4), " samples | S1 = ",
            round.(time_indices[n].S1; digits = 3),
            " | ST = ", round.(time_indices[n].ST; digits = 3))
end

check("the peak size has substantial first-order effects",
      sum(size_indices.S1) > 0.7)
check("the peak time is dominated by interactions",
      sum(time_indices[1000].S1) < 0.5 && all(time_indices[1000].ST .> 0.5))
```

#### C1. Interpret

- For the peak size the first-order indices are about 0.40, 0.27 and 0.25 and add
  to 0.91, so most of the variation is attributable to individual parameters and
  the ranking $\beta > c > \gamma$ is meaningful — as a statement about *these*
  bounds. Widen the $c$ range and the order can change without the model changing.
- For the peak time the first-order indices are near zero, some slightly
  negative, while every total index is around 0.75. That gap is the interaction:
  each parameter is involved in most of the variance, but almost none of it
  belongs to that parameter acting alone.
- So no single parameter drives the timing. Do not push that to "the first-order
  effects are zero": a design of 20,000 samples gives first-order indices near
  $(0.05, 0.01, 0.12)$ summing to about $0.17$, with total indices near $(0.80,
  0.69, 0.74)$.
- $R_0$ alone is not the answer either. Rescaling time as $\tau = \gamma t$ leaves
  a system depending only on $R_0$ and the initial state, so $t_{\text{peak}} =
  F(R_0, u_0)/\gamma$: timing needs a dimensionless ratio, which fixes the shape,
  *and* an absolute rate, which fixes how fast the clock runs. Holding $R_0 = 2$
  and taking $\gamma = 0.125, 0.25, 0.5$ gives peak days of 35.0, 17.5 and 8.75 —
  the same epidemic played at three speeds.
- A first-order index is a variance share and cannot be negative. Seeing $-0.05$
  means the estimator is being asked to resolve something smaller than its own
  noise: the sums are 0.52 at 32 samples, 0.41 at 200 and 0.04 at 1000, which is
  evidence of noise rather than convergence. Before reporting any of it, run
  several design sizes, use a randomized quasi-Monte Carlo design, and quote
  bootstrap intervals rather than point estimates.
- About 19% of the box never grows at all (19.1% in the 20,000 draws), and there
  the peak is at day 0. Which side of that surface a point falls on depends on all
  three parameters at once, so it contributes interaction — but it is not the
  cause, and the peak time does not jump across the surface. It leaves day 0
  continuously.
- The measurement schedule is a separate effect from the epidemic. The model's own
  peak is at 17.52; measured every quarter day it is 17.5, every day 18.0, every
  week 21.0. The first difference belongs to the epidemic and the rest are
  introduced by the schedule. "Which week had the most new cases" is a third
  output again, needing $S(t) - S(t+7)$ rather than a snapshot of $I$: the largest
  weekly window is days 14–21, while instantaneous incidence peaks at day 14.25.
  An output definition can matter a great deal for a reported number and very
  little for a variance decomposition.

### Part D — proving the confounding

Part B showed numerically that $\beta$ and $c$ move the model identically, which
says only that the derivatives agree at one parameter vector.
StructuralIdentifiability answers the question for every trajectory at once, and
symbolically. Nothing below is integrated: `~` records an equation between
symbols.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-d1
using ModelingToolkit
using StructuralIdentifiability
t = ModelingToolkit.t_nounits           # the same time symbol used in Session 1

Logging.disable_logging(Logging.Info)

@parameters b c_rate g k
@variables S(t) I(t) R(t) C(t) y(t)
D = Differential(t)

# A fourth state accumulates infections, and it is that cumulative count which is
# observed. Transmission is written as a plain product of states, so `b * c_rate`
# stands for the effective coefficient κ = βc/N rather than for βc itself.
separate = ODESystem([D(S) ~ -b * c_rate * S * I,
                      D(I) ~ b * c_rate * S * I - g * I,
                      D(R) ~ g * I,
                      D(C) ~ b * c_rate * S * I],
                     t; name = :SIRSeparate)

separate_result = assess_identifiability(
    separate;
    measured_quantities = [y ~ C],
    funcs_to_check = [b, c_rate, g, b * c_rate],
)
separate_result
```

The remedy is not more data of the same kind; it is to stop asking for the two
numbers separately.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-d2
combined = ODESystem([D(S) ~ -k * S * I,
                      D(I) ~ k * S * I - g * I,
                      D(R) ~ g * I,
                      D(C) ~ k * S * I],
                     t; name = :SIRCombined)

combined_result = assess_identifiability(
    combined;
    measured_quantities = [y ~ C],
    funcs_to_check = [k, g],
)
Logging.disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel)

check("β and c are not separately identifiable",
      separate_result[b] == :nonidentifiable &&
      separate_result[c_rate] == :nonidentifiable)
check("their product is identifiable", separate_result[b * c_rate] == :globally)
check("the combined parameter is identifiable",
      get(combined_result, k, :not_asked) == :globally)

combined_result
```

The observation-models chapter leaves a question open: a small epidemic reported
completely and a large one reported partially give case series of similar size,
so can the reporting fraction $\rho$ be separated from transmission? Observe
$\rho C$ rather than $C$, and ask twice.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch14-d3
@parameters rho

Logging.disable_logging(Logging.Warn)

reported = ODESystem([D(S) ~ -k * S * I,
                      D(I) ~ k * S * I - g * I,
                      D(R) ~ g * I,
                      D(C) ~ k * S * I],
                     t; name = :SIRReported)

unknown_initial_state = assess_identifiability(
    reported;
    measured_quantities = [y ~ rho * C],
    funcs_to_check = [rho, k, k / rho, g],
)

# `known_ic` draws a progress bar on stderr; devnull keeps the output clean.
known_initial_state = redirect_stderr(devnull) do
    assess_identifiability(
        reported;
        measured_quantities = [y ~ rho * C],
        funcs_to_check = [rho, k, g],
        known_ic = [S, I, R, C],
    )
end
Logging.disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel)

check("with an unknown initial state, ρ and the transmission rate are confounded",
      unknown_initial_state[rho] == :nonidentifiable &&
      unknown_initial_state[k] == :nonidentifiable)
check("what survives is their ratio, not their product",
      unknown_initial_state[k / rho] == :globally)
check("knowing the initial state makes ρ identifiable",
      known_initial_state[rho] == :globally && known_initial_state[k] == :globally)

(; unknown_initial_state, known_initial_state)
```

#### D1. Interpret

- Nothing was learnt about the world, and that is the point. The observation
  determines one transmission coefficient; asking for the two factors separately
  is asking the data a question it cannot answer, and an optimizer handed that
  question will still return two numbers.
- What was gained is a model whose parameters match what the data can determine.
  What was given up is the interpretation: $k$ is not a contact rate, and no fit
  of this model can report one.
- To the colleague who "estimated the contact rate at 9.4 per day": ask what else
  was in the model and what was observed. If $\beta$ and $c$ both appear and only
  incidence was seen, 9.4 is whatever the optimizer stopped at along a flat
  direction — it is determined by the starting guess and the stopping rule, not by
  the data. Ask for the product, or for the profile.
- The reporting fraction changes status between the two runs with no new data
  because identifiability is a property of the model *and* the observation *and*
  what is assumed known. With an unknown initial state $\rho$ and $k$ are
  confounded and only the ratio $k/\rho$ survives; declaring the initial state
  known makes both identifiable.
- The unknown-initial-state case is much closer to an outbreak analysis, where the
  number already infected at the first report is exactly what nobody knows. So
  identifiability came from background knowledge, not from the data.
- This is a *structural* result: it says the information is present in a
  noiseless, continuously observed curve, not that forty noisy daily counts will
  pin $\rho$ down. That gap is practical identifiability. Note also that marking
  only $C(0)$ as known does not work, because the package reports identifiability
  for *generic* known values and $C(0) = 0$ is not generic.
